name: Western Australia
summary_text: Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Visitors in every state, Western Australia included, stand under that national framework, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.  State protection in Western Australia runs through a narrower formulation. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects the attribute 'gender history', defined by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex, and the official WA Government guidance states that a person has gender history where they identify as a member of the opposite sex by living or seeking to live as such. Direct discrimination, including treating a person as their former sex, and indirect discrimination are both unlawful under the Act. The binary, medically-inflected wording means a non-binary or gender-nonconforming visitor may fall outside the state-law definition and would rely on federal coverage for a state-level complaint. Western Australia has no state anti-vilification offence, civil or criminal, and no statutory charter binding public authorities.  Complaint eligibility under the state attribute has historically been tied to recognition certificates or a registry change through the Births, Deaths and Marriages framework. On 16 April 2024 Premier Roger Cook and Attorney-General John Quigley announced the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024, which repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, described by the ministers as the only remaining board of its kind in Australia. The Board's functions move to a streamlined administrative process within the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and applicants are no longer required to undergo medical or surgical reassignment. A statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, now suffices, and a 'non-binary' sex descriptor becomes available. Stricter rules apply to under-18s through parental consent or Family Court of WA permission, and the Act contains a statutory review clause after three years. The reform implements the WA Law Reform Commission's 2018 recommendations.  The registration reform reshapes the state discrimination attribute itself. The Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet records that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 amends section 4(1) of the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. The Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001, does not operate retrospectively, and commences by proclamation; once it is in force, gender history complaints must comply with the new registration requirements.  Two complaint routes exist and only one may be used. A complaint may be lodged with the WA Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 within 12 months, with acknowledgment of receipt within a week and a free conciliation conference to follow, or with the Australian Human Rights Commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 within 24 months, reduced to 12 months for employment matters. Choosing one route forecloses the other.  Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere in the world: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity in Western Australia, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held nationally since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.  Counterweights are documented. The Tickle case grew out of organised exclusionary activism, and ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and records, and pressure to roll back existing rights, alongside systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people.

name: Saint Barthélemy
summary_text: Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.  No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies.  Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is delivered on an island of about 8 square miles with roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against Saint Barthélemy in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access; prescriptions and ongoing treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally.  Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. French prison administration policy recognises only biological sex for placement, and trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex; a 2011 case in Nantes placed a trans woman in a men's prison. Detainees held in Saint Barthélemy fall under that same system. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.  An aggregate index rates the collectivity 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag.  Socially the territory is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors.

sources.title: Vichy Article 334 / Article 331 - unequal age of consent law
sources.documents: Former discriminatory age of consent (21 then 18 for homosexual relations vs 15 for heterosexual); documents repeal and equalization relevant to sexual-offences enforcement history.
sources.detail: No URL visible; citation detail: introduced 6 Aug 1942 as article 334, moved to article 331 on 8 Feb 1945, lowered to 18 in 1974, repealed 4 Aug 1982 under President Francois Mitterrand to equalise at 15
